title: DAVID HAD MANY WOMEN—YET SCRIPTURE MAKES A POINT OF SAYING HE DIDN’T SLEEP WITH ABISHAG
paragraphs:
DAVID HAD MANY WOMEN—YET SCRIPTURE MAKES A POINT OF SAYING HE DIDN’T SLEEP WITH ABISHAG
The man who once took another man’s wife was eventually placed beside an exceedingly beautiful woman—and Scripture stopped to tell us what did not happen.
There is one sentence near the end of David’s life that is incredibly easy to read past.
Four Hebrew words.
Quiet words.
No battlefield. No giant. No adultery exposed by a prophet. No murdered husband. No dead child. No rebellious son. No public humiliation.
Just an old king lying in a cold room with a beautiful young woman beside him.
And then Scripture says:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
Veha-melekh lo yeda‘ah.
“And the king did not know her.”
—1 Kings 1:4
In biblical Hebrew, yada‘—“to know”—can describe ordinary knowledge, but in this kind of context it is a recognized biblical way of referring to sexual relations.
In other words:
David did not sleep with Abishag.
And that sentence becomes astonishing when you remember who David was.
This was not a man whose history with women was spotless.
This was David.
David had wives.
David had concubines.
David had known sexual desire.
David had also catastrophically abused power in connection with Bathsheba.
He saw her.
He wanted her.
He sent for her.
He took her.
And when her pregnancy threatened to expose what he had done, David eventually arranged circumstances that resulted in Uriah's death.
The Bible does not airbrush that scandal.
That matters.
Scripture refuses to turn its heroes into plastic saints.
David could write psalms and still sin terribly.
He could defeat Goliath and still be defeated by his own desires.
He could be courageous before armies and dangerously weak in private.
He could genuinely love God and still commit sins that brought devastating consequences upon himself and others.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because we prefer testimonies where the darkness is far enough in the past that we can safely applaud the ending.
But David’s story does something more painful.
It shows us what sin can destroy.
Then it shows us what repentance looks like when excuses finally die.
And years later, when David is old and physically failing, Scripture places another woman beside him.
Not merely a woman.
The narrator deliberately tells us:
וְהַנַּעֲרָה יָפָה עַד־מְאֹד
Veha-na‘arah yafah ‘ad-me’od.
“The young woman was exceedingly beautiful.”
Her name was Abishag the Shunammite.

David had become so old that clothing could no longer keep him warm. His servants therefore searched for a young virgin who could attend him and lie close to him so that her body warmth might warm the aging king.
They searched throughout Israel.
They found Abishag.
She entered David’s chamber.
She served him.
She remained physically close to him.
She was exceedingly beautiful.
Then Scripture gives us that strange, deliberate sentence:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
“But the king did not know her.”
Why tell us?
Why does the narrator care that we know what did not happen?
We should be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly say, “God placed Abishag there as David’s final temptation.”
It does not tell us that this scene was a divinely arranged test designed to prove David’s repentance.
We should not claim more than Scripture claims.
Nor should we romanticize David's earlier sexual history. The biblical narratives surrounding his household contain enormous dysfunction, grief, violence, rivalry, and consequences.
But the narrator unquestionably wants us to know one particular fact about Abishag:
David did not have sexual relations with her.
That fact becomes especially striking because readers already know David’s history.
Once, David stood on a rooftop and saw a beautiful woman.
Later, David lay in a bed with another beautiful woman close enough to warm his failing body.
Once, desire became taking.
Here, proximity did not become intercourse.
And somewhere between those two scenes lies a lifetime of scars.
Bathsheba.
Uriah.
Nathan.
A dead child.
A fractured household.
Amnon.
Tamar.
Absalom.
Rebellion.
Grief.
David learned something many of us learn far too late:
Sin can be forgiven without becoming harmless.
Grace does not mean consequences were imaginary.
David's repentance did not resurrect Uriah.
It did not erase Bathsheba’s suffering.
It did not magically repair every fracture in his family.
Forgiveness is not God pretending evil was acceptable.
Forgiveness is God refusing to let evil have the final word over the repentant sinner.
And that is where David's story begins reaching through the centuries and touching ours.
Because perhaps your name is not David.
Perhaps your scandal never became public.
Perhaps nobody confronted you with the words Nathan spoke to David:
“You are the man.”
Maybe your battlefield is a phone screen nobody else sees.
A private conversation.
A relationship you know is crossing boundaries.
Pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
Bitterness you have learned to disguise as discernment.
Money you should not be touching.
Attention you secretly crave.
An emotional affair you insist is “just friendship.”
A habit you keep renaming because calling it sin would require repentance.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing well spiritually.
You worship.
You post Scripture.
You encourage people.
You know Christian vocabulary.
But there is a room inside your life where you keep telling Jesus:
“Not this one.”
David's story will not let us comfortably divide humanity into good people and scandalous people.
The Gospel gives us a more devastating diagnosis.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
David needed one.
You need one.
I need one.
And Christianity's answer is not simply, “Try harder than David did.”
Its answer is Jesus Christ.
David was Israel's king.
But David was never Israel's final King.
He was a shepherd, but another Shepherd was coming.
He defeated enemies, but another Son of David would defeat the enemies David could never conquer for us: sin and death.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus came to purchase it.
David's hands were stained.
Christ's hands were pierced.
David sometimes used royal power for himself.
Jesus Christ, the rightful King, humbled Himself and gave Himself for sinners.
At the cross, God does not tell us that our sins do not matter.
The cross tells us they matter so much that redemption cost blood.
And yet it also tells us something almost impossible to believe when shame has been whispering in your ear for years:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That does not make your sin small.
It makes Christ's grace enormous.
David understood something of this long before Calvary when, after Nathan confronted him, he stopped constructing defenses and cried to God.
Psalm 51 preserves the language of a shattered man:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Notice what David wanted.
Not merely a cleaner reputation.
A clean heart.
Not better public relations.
Transformation.
Not “Help everyone forget.”
“God, change me.”
That is repentance.
Repentance is more than being embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is more than regretting consequences.
It is coming into agreement with God about your sin and turning toward Him for mercy and transformation.
And perhaps that is why the Abishag sentence can hit so hard.
The Bible remembered David's Bathsheba chapter.
But David was not frozen forever at the worst thing he had done.
Read that again.
David was not frozen forever at the worst thing he had done.
Neither does Scripture pretend the worst thing never happened.
That balance is the beauty of biblical grace.
Grace tells the truth about yesterday without surrendering tomorrow to yesterday.
Some people live as though repentance cannot possibly change anything because they have already failed too badly.
Others talk about grace as though repentance changes nothing because forgiveness means continuing exactly as before.
The Gospel permits neither lie.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus forgives sinners.
And Jesus transforms sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
The question becomes whether you are willing to walk out.
There may eventually come a moment when the old temptation stands close again.
Same smell.
Same opportunity.
Same loneliness.
Same secret access.
Same type of person.
Same trigger.
Same late-night vulnerability.
And suddenly you discover whether you merely regretted the consequences...
or whether God has been changing your heart.
Sometimes one of the most beautiful testimonies is not what somebody finally does.
It is what, by God's grace, they no longer do.
Nobody applauds because you closed the browser.
Nobody sees that you deleted the number.
Nobody knows you walked away.
Nobody realizes you could have taken the money and didn't.
Nobody hears the message you decided not to send.
Nobody knows what was available behind the closed door.
Nobody celebrates the temptation you refused.
But heaven does not need an audience before obedience matters.
There are victories that make no noise.
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ.
The king did not know her.
Four Hebrew words.
Yet for someone reading this while fighting an old version of themselves, they can sound like thunder.
Your past may explain why temptation recognizes your address.
It does not have the authority to own the house forever.
You may have been the adulterer.
The liar.
The addict.
The hypocrite.
The angry father.
The unfaithful spouse.
The compromised believer.
The person who knew better and still did it.
Repentance does not require pretending otherwise.
But if you belong to Christ, neither should you build your permanent identity around the sin from which Christ came to redeem you.
Paul wrote that if anyone is in Christ, there is new creation.
Not reputation management.
Not religious cosmetics.
New creation.
And that means perhaps someone reading this needs to stop saying:
“This is simply who I am.”
No.
Maybe it is what you have repeatedly done.
Maybe it has been your pattern for fifteen years.
Maybe you have failed so often that freedom sounds naïve.
But Jesus Christ did not walk out of a tomb so that your favorite sin could write your biography forever.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Seek accountability where necessary.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Put boundaries around the places where you repeatedly fall.
Stop protecting what is killing you.
And run toward Christ.
Not after you become clean.
Run to Him because you cannot cleanse yourself.
That is the Gospel.
We do not wash ourselves sufficiently and then approach Jesus.
We approach Jesus because sinners need washing.
There is another important reason Abishag matters.
Immediately after Scripture tells us David did not know her sexually, the story turns toward succession and the throne.
David is dying.
Adonijah begins positioning himself as king.
Eventually Abishag herself becomes entangled in the royal succession crisis when Adonijah asks to receive her as his wife.
So 1 Kings 1:4 is not merely an inspirational sentence about sexual restraint. It also helps establish Abishag's relationship to David as the narrative moves into a dangerous struggle over kingship.
That context protects us from turning the passage into a motivational slogan.
But it does not make the contrast with David's history disappear.
The Bible wants us to remember the whole David.
Giant killer.
Psalmist.
King.
Adulterer.
Repentant sinner.
Broken father.
Worshiper.
Old man.
A deeply flawed servant of God whose life kept pointing beyond himself toward the King humanity actually needed.
Jesus.
Because David cannot save you.
David cannot save David.
Only Christ can save sinners.
And perhaps this article found you at precisely the uncomfortable moment when you are tired of performing Christianity while privately negotiating with something Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Then do not merely admire David's restraint with Abishag.
Go deeper.
Remember David on the floor of repentance.
Remember Psalm 51.
Remember the Son of David carrying a cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy God coming for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe today your prayer needs to become painfully simple:
Jesus, no more hiding.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, create a clean heart in me.
Jesus, teach me to hate what is destroying me and love what pleases You.
Jesus, rewrite what sin tried to make permanent.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers the private details. But you can make a small public declaration that you are finished pretending.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
Not to expose them.
To remind them that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
and a Savior who is greater than all of it.
Save it as well.
Because old temptations have a strange habit of returning after powerful moments of conviction have faded.
You may need these words again on a weaker night.
Gospel Warrior exists because biblical truth should not merely fill timelines.
It should make disciples.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor.
But generosity, partnership, and willingly helping sound Gospel ministry reach more people can genuinely be acts through which believers seek to glorify God.
It is mission.
It is helping truth travel.
It is helping another exhausted believer find Scripture at midnight.
Another ashamed sinner discover that repentance is still possible.
Another wandering Christian remember the cross.
Another person encounter Jesus.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
Share because somebody else may desperately need the truth you almost scrolled past.
Tag because sometimes one name placed beneath one message becomes the doorway to one necessary conversation.
Save because conviction should survive longer than a moment.
Follow because discipleship requires more than occasional inspiration.
And above everything else...
Come to Christ.
David's story is not ultimately beautiful because David eventually behaved better around Abishag.
It is beautiful because Scripture tells the truth about sinners while continually directing our hope toward the God who redeems them.
The Bible did not erase David's scandal.
God's grace did something greater.
It refused to let scandal have the last word.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needs to carry away from this today:
The chapter you are most ashamed to remember may still become the place from which you spend the rest of your life remembering how desperately you needed Jesus.
